title: Breakouts before photos
body: I used to cancel plans when I woke up with a new breakout. Group photos were the worst: I would stand at the edge, chin tilted down, already apologising in my head. Last month my cousin's engagement came around and I decided to just go. I covered what I wanted to cover and left the rest. Nobody looked at my chin the way I did. Looking at the photos later, what I noticed was my own smile, which I had not seen in a picture for a long time.

title: Not a shade to fix
body: Growing up I was told to stay out of the sun, to carry an umbrella to school, to be careful which colours I wore. Nobody said it cruelly. It was just the air in the house. When my grandmother passed, I found her old saris and wore one to a wedding. In the mirror I finally saw her warmth in my own skin and it was not something to correct. I am still unlearning the umbrella, but I am doing it on days I choose.

title: Where I healed
body: I had chickenpox at nine and the marks on my forehead became the first thing I covered with a fringe. For years I arranged my hair around them like a curtain. At twenty-two I cut the fringe on a whim and the world did not end. These days I think of those marks as proof that my skin knows how to repair itself. They are not a flaw I am hiding, they are a place where something hurt and then got better.

title: The filter I deleted
body: I deleted the filter app on a Tuesday after catching myself retouching a photo I was only going to send to my sister. It took about a week for my own face to feel familiar again, which says something. Every unfiltered selfie felt wrong and slightly cruel, like a stranger had been swapped in. By the second week it just looked like me. Tired, a bit shiny, and mine.

title: Melasma and mornings
body: My patches darken every summer and soften a little in winter, like a tide. For two years I asked the internet how to erase them and came away with a shelf of products and a lot of shame. This year I changed the question. I stopped asking how to get rid of them and started asking how to be gentle with myself while they are here. Mornings are easier now. I wash my face, I say good morning, and I leave it there.

title: Adult acne
body: Nobody warned me that acne could arrive at thirty. I had survived my teens with clear skin and quietly assumed I was done. Then a new job, new stress, and suddenly I was hiding behind my hair in meetings. What helped was a friend who simply said, me too, and showed me her own jawline without any filter or fuss. I am learning that it is common, that it can be treated, and that it is not a verdict on how I take care of myself.

title: Scrolling less
body: I muted every account that made me feel smaller, one by one, without drama. I did not unfollow anyone, because I did not want to make it a statement. I just stopped seeing them. My feed is quieter now and so is my head. I still see beautiful faces, but fewer of them arrive with a quiet instruction attached.

title: Acne scars, honestly
body: I spent years chasing perfectly smooth skin and my bathroom drawer shows it. A friend looked at my cheek in daylight and said it looks like the moon, and strangely that stuck. I stopped treating the chase as the goal. Some days I treat my scars, some days I just say hello to them. Both feel like care, and neither one feels like losing.

title: Seeing myself in colour
body: For a long time I looked for beauty that looked like me and did not find it on the posters, in the films, or in the shop windows. So I started noticing it where it was: in my aunt laughing with her head thrown back, in my cousin's wedding photographs, in my father's hands. After a while the noticing turned inward. I am not there yet, but I can now catch the moment I am about to apologise for my colour and decide not to.

title: Freckles, finally
body: I hid my freckles for years under heavy foundation, even to go to the shop. Then a child on the bus told me, very seriously, that I had stars on my nose. A stranger later called them constellations. I let that be true. I do not wear foundation every day any more, and on the days I do, I leave my nose bare.

title: A note to keep
body: I wrote this on a sticky note and put it on the mirror: the face I see here is a person, not a project. I can let it be here with me today. It does not fix anything. But on mornings when I stand there auditing myself, it reminds me that I am allowed to just brush my teeth and go.

title: The whole picture
body: I used to look for one mark before I saw anything else in a photo, a patch by my temple that felt like a spotlight. Little by little I am training my eyes to travel. The light on the window behind me. The way my hair does that thing. The people I am with. The mark is still there, but it is no longer the whole picture, and some days I forget to look for it.

title: Under my eyes
body: Dark circles run in my family, and I have had them since I was a teenager. People kept asking me if I was okay, if I had slept, if I was ill. They meant well, but after the hundredth time I started to hear it as you look wrong. I now answer, I am fine, this is just my face. Saying it out loud, lightly, took some of the sting out of the question.

title: Concealer as armour
body: For years I would not leave the house without concealer under my eyes. It was armour, and I do not think that is silly. Armour is useful. What I am practising now is choosing days to go without, such as the supermarket on a Sunday or a walk before work. Nobody has fainted. I am learning which days I want armour and which days I just want to be unguarded and comfortable.

title: Before the video call
body: The small square of my own face in video calls undoes me. I used to spend ten minutes before every meeting staring at it, adjusting the light and my angle. Hiding self-view helped more than any ring light. When I cannot see myself, I can listen. It took me a month to notice that nobody else in the call was studying my face either. They were looking at their own squares too.

title: Edited, and everyone knew
body: My friend posted a photo with her skin smoothed and lightened a few shades. Everyone commented how flawless she looked. Weeks later she admitted she had hated that photo because it did not look like her. That was the day I understood how much of what I compare myself to is not real, even to the people in it. Now when I feel the old pull, I ask myself who this picture was made for.
